explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. Verse 2 says, “May he judge Your people with righteousness and Your afflicted with justice.” So the justice and righteousness from verse 1 go straight to work. I think that's a prayer for a king who uses what he's been given. A gift sitting in the box does nobody any good.

Close to a king's job, but that's not on this list. Verse 2 asks for the king to judge God's people with righteousness and God's afflicted with justice. This prayer doesn't mention building anything. I'd have picked the shiny construction project too, so no shame here.

I get why a king and armies go together in your head. But verse 2 doesn't ask for that. It asks for the king to judge God's people with righteousness and the afflicted with justice. This prayer is about how he treats people, not who he commands.
That's one of the two. Verse 4 asks for the king to “save the children of the needy.” Notice who gets the king's attention here. It's the kids of the needy, not the people with the fanciest hats.

Yes, this one goes in the second blank. The verse asks for the king to “crush the oppressor.” The words come right after the part about saving the children of the needy. The prayer asks for the king to stand up for the afflicted and to deal with the one hurting them.

A warning is a polite word, and verse 4 isn't being polite. It asks for the king to “crush the oppressor.” That's much stronger than a heads-up. Good news is that the other blank, “save,” belongs to the children of the needy.

Ignoring the needy is the one thing this prayer is trying to avoid. Verse 4 asks for the king to “save the children of the needy and crush the oppressor.” Nobody gets brushed off in that line. It's the opposite of looking away.

Pardoning sounds gentle, but that's not the word in verse 4. The prayer asks for the king to “crush the oppressor.” The children of the needy get saved. I think the blank for the oppressor wants a much heavier word than pardon.

One generation is too short for this prayer. Verse 5 asks for the king to be feared “as long as the sun shines, as long as the moon remains, through all generations.” That's sun, moon AND every generation. This prayer doesn't think small, friend.

Right, it's False. Verse 5 says, “May they fear him as long as the sun shines, as long as the moon remains, through all generations.” The prayer asks for it to last through all generations, not one. Sun and moon are the timekeepers here, and I'd say they have a long shift.

Yes! Verse 7 says, “May the righteous flourish in his days.” After the spring showers in verse 6, I think it makes sense. Rain falls and things grow, and the prayer pictures the righteous growing under this king like grass after a good rain.

Struggling doesn't fit with spring showers, friend. Verse 7 asks for the righteous to “flourish in his days.” Rain is falling on the earth in verse 6, so things are growing, not wilting. Picture a garden after a good rain.

Scattering is more like a bag of sprinkles hitting the floor. Verse 7 asks for the righteous to “flourish in his days.” After the rain in verse 6, the picture is growth. Everyone stays put and gets better.

explanations.answer: To the ends of the earth
explanations.explanation: That's it. Verse 8 says, “May he rule from sea to sea, and from the Euphrates to the ends of the earth.” That's a big map. I once thought my bakery counter was a lot of room to cover.

The Jordan is a real river, but verse 8 goes way past it. It says, “May he rule from sea to sea, and from the Euphrates to the ends of the earth.” The prayer doesn't stop at one river. It goes all the way to the ends of the earth.

That's a lot smaller than what this prayer asks for. Verse 8 says, “May he rule from sea to sea, and from the Euphrates to the ends of the earth.” No walls are mentioned. I think anyone drawing this map would run out of paper.

That's right. Verse 10 says, “May the kings of Tarshish and distant shores bring tribute; may the kings of Sheba and Seba offer gifts.” These are kings from far-off places coming with their hands full. The prayer asks for the whole world to show up with something to give.

You're picturing a whole fleet showing up, friend. But verse 10 says the kings from Tarshish and distant shores bring “tribute,” and the kings of Sheba and Seba offer “gifts.” No soldiers are mentioned. I think they came to give, not to fight.

I'd be nervous to open that mail. Verse 10 asks for the kings of Tarshish and distant shores to bring “tribute,” and for the kings of Sheba and Seba to offer “gifts.” Nothing about warnings. Just gifts, and kings carrying them.
True. Verse 11 says, “May all kings bow down to him and all nations serve him.” The kings from distant shores are just the start. The prayer widens to ALL kings and all nations.
It's True, friend. Verse 11 says, “May all kings bow down to him and all nations serve him.” After the kings from distant shores, the prayer asks for all of them. That's a lot of crowns bowing.

explanations.answer: Deliver the needy who cry out
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. Verse 12 says, “For he will deliver the needy who cry out and the afflicted who have no helper.” After all the bowing and gifts, the prayer turns to the needy. I think that's the part worth remembering.

explanations.answer: Tax the poor who cry out
explanations.explanation: Whoa, no. That's the opposite of verse 12. It says, “For he will deliver the needy who cry out and the afflicted who have no helper.” When the needy cry out, this king delivers them.

The kings did bring gifts, so I see why you'd go there. But verse 12 turns in a new direction. It says, “For he will deliver the needy who cry out and the afflicted who have no helper.” Nothing here about rewarding the kings.
I'd want that to be false too, and it is. Verse 12 says he will deliver “the afflicted who have no helper.” No helper means nobody in their corner, and the king helps them anyway.
Right, it's False. Verse 12 says he will deliver “the needy who cry out and the afflicted who have no helper.” The ones with no helper are exactly the ones he helps. Nobody has to bring a connection.

explanations.answer: Their blood is precious to him
explanations.explanation: That's the reason. Verse 14 says, “He will redeem them from oppression and violence, for their blood is precious in his sight.” Their lives matter to him. That's the reason the text gives, and it's a good one.

Tribute shows up in verse 10, but it's not the reason here. Verse 14 says, “He will redeem them from oppression and violence, for their blood is precious in his sight.” The oppressed aren't buying his help. Their lives are precious to him.

The text gives a different reason. Verse 14 says, “He will redeem them from oppression and violence, for their blood is precious in his sight.” No army is mentioned. They're precious to him just as they are.
That's right. Verse 15 says, “May people ever pray for him; may they bless him all day long.” All day long is a lot of blessing. Even my oven timer takes breaks.

Once a year is a pretty short list, friend. Verse 15 asks for people to “bless him all day long.” That's not a calendar thing, it's from morning to night. A yearly blessing would be easy to forget, like a tax form.

Feast days are nice, but verse 15 doesn't limit it. It says, “May people ever pray for him; may they bless him all day long.” The prayer doesn't mention any special days. It asks for blessing all day long.
Yes! Verse 16 says, “May there be an abundance of grain in the land; may it sway atop the hills.” That's more than a little. When grain grows on the hilltops, there's plenty to go around.

Just enough is a careful ask, and this prayer isn't being careful. Verse 16 says, “May there be an abundance of grain in the land.” An abundance means more than enough. Grain swaying on the hills is a lot of grain.
Verse 16 doesn't say that. It asks for “an abundance of grain in the land.” It's about the whole land, not one pantry. Grain on the hills means the whole country has plenty.
True. Verse 17 says, “In him may all nations be blessed; may they call him blessed.” All nations, not just one. This prayer has a very wide reach.
It's True, friend. Verse 17 says, “In him may all nations be blessed; may they call him blessed.” It's not one nation or two. It asks for all nations.
That's not what verse 18 says. It blesses “the LORD God, the God of Israel, who alone does marvelous deeds.” The word is “alone.” The prayer gives the marvelous deeds to the LORD, not the king.

Right, it's False. Verse 18 says, “Blessed be the LORD God, the God of Israel, who alone does marvelous deeds.” The key word is “alone.” The king is prayed for all through this psalm, but the marvelous deeds belong to the LORD alone.

That's right. Verse 19 says, “may all the earth be filled with His glory.” After the prayer asked for a king to rule to the ends of the earth, it ends asking for the earth to be filled with the LORD's glory. Now that's a big finish.

The heavens do sound glorious, friend. But verse 19 says, “may all the earth be filled with His glory.” The word is earth. The prayer ends by looking at all the earth, the same earth where the king's name was meant to last.

A temple would be a nice place to be filled with glory, but it's not what the verse says. Verse 19 says, “may all the earth be filled with His glory.” It's the whole earth. Not one building, just everywhere.
